Sonnet. A fourteen-line poem in iambic pentameter structured by a particular rhyme scheme and argument. Originating in thirteenth-century Italy with Petrarch, the form became a vehicle for exploring love, time, mortality, and philosophical inquiry. The sonnet achieved its English apotheosis with Shakespeare and represents the intersection of literary and musical formalism. Its rhyme scheme and meter create an architecture for thought itself.

The Petrarchan sonnet, also called the Italian sonnet, divides into octave and sestet. Eight lines with the rhyme scheme ABBAABBA followed by six lines with a similar pattern, creating a volta or turn between statement and response. The Shakespearean sonnet, the English sonnet, follows three quatrains and a couplet with the rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. This allows for a more dramatic final reversal in the closing couplet.

Shakespeare composed one hundred fifty-four sonnets exploring love, procreation, beauty, time, and absence. Collectively they present a philosophical meditation on desire and mortality. The sonnet form's strict constraints—meter, rhyme, line count—create what aestheticians call the freedom of form. The paradox is that rigid structure enables philosophical depth. Sonnets were often composed in sequences: connected poems exploring a single relationship or theme. This represents a proto-novelistic form that influenced later narrative poetry.

The form's musical dimension extends beyond meter. Sonnets were set to music, particularly as madrigals, creating a hybrid of verbal and musical artistry. The sonnet remains the most influential closed form in English poetry, surviving centuries of modernist and postmodern challenges to its conventions.

William Shakespeare is the author of the one hundred fifty-four sonnets that defined the English form. Petrarch is the Italian poet who invented the sonnet form and established its thematic preoccupations. The English Renaissance is the period when the sonnet became central to English poetic practice. Iambic pentameter is the metrical foundation of sonnets, creating a ten-syllable rhythmic line. The madrigal is the musical form that often set sonnetic texts, particularly Italian poetry. Poetry is the broader genre of which the sonnet is a defining subform. Love poetry is the traditional subject matter of sonnets, though expanded to philosophy and temporality.
